summary: Extends the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) from RFC 5070 so phishing incidents can be reported. The extensions cover information from the first phishing lure through to taking down the site that collects stolen data, and support simple reports or full forensic reports. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Phishing means tricking people into giving up secrets. This gives a standard form for telling others about such tricks, so they can be stopped faster.

questions: how to report phishing in iodef
what fraud types does iodef support
subtitle: A standard XML extension for sharing reports about phishing, from the first lure to the takedown of the site that collects stolen credentials.

tldr.problem: Groups that fight phishing each use their own formats and tools, so sharing and correlating data about one attack becomes slow and hard to automate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5901 adds a PhraudReport element to the IODEF incident format from RFC 5070. It records the lure, its source, the sensor that detected it, the collection site, any takedown and related evidence.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard. Reports can be small (a few required fields) or full forensic records, and several events can be combined in one incident report.

today: RFC 5901 is a Proposed Standard from July 2010, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5070.

sections.title: Why a Common Phishing Report Format
sections.content:
RFC 5901 defines an extension to the Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) from RFC 5070. It describes phishing, and other fraud, as broadly launched social engineering attacks that trick people into revealing credentials such as passwords, account numbers or ATM PINs. The text uses "phishing" and "fraud" interchangeably.

The motivation is coordination. As more service providers and investigators share data, party-specific tools and formats multiply until they overwhelm those parties. A common format makes it easier to correlate information from many sources and to automate analysis, which speeds up response.

The RFC reuses the IODEF data model rather than inventing a new report format, and adds only the structures needed for phishing and e-crime. How reports are exchanged and the political side of sharing are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If every detective wrote notes in a different language, they could not compare them. A shared notebook format lets everyone read each other's notes quickly.

sections.title: The Parts of a Fraud Event
sections.content:
The RFC defines its terms first. Phishing is the whole process of identifying victims, contacting them with a lure, getting them to send private credentials to a collection site, and storing those credentials. A fraud event is phishing plus the later fraudulent use of the credentials. A lure is the decoy, and it includes a pointer to a collection site, which may be a website, email box, SMS number or phone number. A lure can travel by any messaging medium, not just email.

A fraud event has at least six components: the fraudster, the attack source, the lure, the victim, the credentials and the collection site. Two more come from a holistic view: the sensor that detected the phish (an intrusion detection system, firewall, filter, email gateway or human analyst) and a forensic or archive site where an investigator kept a copy of the evidence.

Useful data falls into four groups: data about the lure, data about the collection site, detection information (knowing how something was detected helps build better detection) and analysis output from investigators.
sections.eli5: A phishing trick has a sneaky sender, a fake message, a person who gets fooled and a hiding place where the stolen secrets land. Someone spotting the trick and someone keeping copies of the evidence are part of the story too.

sections.title: How a Fraud Report Is Built
sections.content:
A fraud activity report is an IODEF-Document with an Incident element. The phishing-specific fields sit in a PhraudReport element inside the AdditionalData element of EventData, using the extension procedure in Section 5 of RFC 5070. Several PhraudReports can be combined in one EventData, and several EventData elements in one incident report.

There are three kinds of report, marked with the ext-purpose attribute of the Incident: a new report (empty or create), an update (update), for example to add new collection sites or takedown information, and a request to delete a report that was in error (delete). The RFC calls this marking advisory, because operating procedures for a report's life cycle are very environment specific.

A report MUST pass XML validation against the schema from RFC 5070 and the extensions in Appendix A of this document.
sections.eli5: A report is a folder with a special phishing page tucked inside. You can mark the folder as new, as an update, or as 'please throw this one away, we made a mistake'.

sections.title: The PhraudReport Element
sections.content:
The PhraudReport carries a required Version attribute, whose value must be 0.06 to comply with the RFC, and a required FraudType attribute. The FraudType decides what the optional FraudParameter holds, such as the subject line of a phishing email, a lure message or a website. The listed types are phishing, recruiting (recruiting money mules), malware distribution, fraudulent site, dnsspoof, archive, other, unknown and an ext-value choice for types not predefined.

Beneath it are elements for a common name for the fraud (PhishNameRef), a local name or identifier (PhishNameLocalRef), the defrauded brand (FraudedBrandName), the lure source, the originating sensor, the collection site (DCSite), takedown information, archived data, related data, correlation data, comments and the raw email (EmailRecord).

A specific phish can be identified by combining FraudType, FraudParameter, FraudedBrandName, LureSource and PhishNameRef.
sections.eli5: The main page asks what kind of trick this was, what it was called and which company's name was faked, then has boxes for the details.

sections.title: Lure, Sensor, Collection Site and Takedown
sections.content:
LureSource is required. It holds one or more System entries (a real IP address if known, or a spoofed one with the spoofed attribute set), optional DomainData (registration dates, nameservers, contacts and a status), and optional records of included malware, downloaded files and modified Windows registry keys. Contacts carry a Confidence value: known-fraudulent, looks-fraudulent, known-real, looks-real or unknown. A system's status can be spoofed, fraudulent, innocent-hacked, innocent-hijacked or unknown.

Included malware may be identified by name and by a hash Reference (implementations SHOULD support SHA-1). The malware itself may be attached as hex data, XORed with a pattern so that it is rendered harmless. The default pattern is 0x55AA55AA55AA55BB.

OriginatingSensor is required and says what detected the activity: web, webgateway, mailgateway, browser, ispsensor, human, honeypot or other. It also needs the date the sensor first saw the activity.

DCSite describes the collection site. Its DCType is web, email, keylogger, automation or unspecified, and its content is a URL, domain, email address, IP address or other identifier. A confidence attribute from 0 to 100 states how sure the reporter is, where 0 is a false positive and 100 means independently verified.

TakeDownInfo records who removed, disabled or blocked the collection site and when. ArchivedData points to, or embeds in base64, a copy of site contents. EmailRecord holds the number of emails seen and, optionally, the whole message with full headers as one string.
sections.eli5: The report says where the fake message came from, how it was caught, where victims were told to send their secrets, and who shut that place down. For many answers it also says how sure the reporter is.

sections.title: Required Elements
sections.content:
A compliant report SHALL contain the elements IODEF itself requires on an Incident (IncidentID, ReportTime, Assessment with Impact, Contact, and EventData with DetectTime and AdditionalData). Within the PhraudReport it SHALL contain the FraudType and Version attributes, a LureSource with an iodef:System, and an OriginatingSensor with a DateFirstSeen and an iodef:System.

The RFC admits that this makes a quite sparse report. The originator SHOULD include any detail learned from the analysis, because volatile information may not be recoverable later and may help with investigation or with correlation to other events. Sensitive values can be marked with the restriction parameter of each data element.
sections.eli5: There is a short list of boxes you must fill in. But you are asked to fill in as many extra boxes as you can, because clues can disappear later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The format is merely a data representation, so it does not directly introduce security issues. But parties exchanging reports will have concerns, so the message format and transport MUST ensure the appropriate confidentiality, integrity and authenticity for the environment. The main risks named are that reports may be falsified or corrupted in transit. Where transmission security is questionable, a digital signature and/or encryption on each report counters both.

The RFC also cautions about the iodef:restriction attribute. A reporter should not mark elements private or need-to-know unless the receiver can safeguard them as marked. For instance, it asks whether a collector URL in a private PhraudReport may go on a distributed block list, gives no answer and urges exchanging parties to agree on common marking rules.
sections.eli5: Notes about a crime should not be forged or smudged on the way, so lock or sign them. And if you stamp a page 'secret', make sure the person you give it to knows how to keep it secret.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC asks for two registrations under the registry mechanism in RFC 3688: the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-phish-1.0 and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:iodef-phish-1.0. The schema itself is given in Appendix A of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks for an official name tag for the new form, so nobody else uses the same tag.

items.label: phishing
items.desc: Standard phishing lure; FraudParameter is the lure subject line or message.

items.label: recruiting
items.desc: Recruit, or mule, email or message.

items.label: malware distribution
items.desc: Lure that leads the recipient to an infected site.

items.label: fraudulent site
items.desc: Known fraudulent site used to show lures.

items.label: dnsspoof
items.desc: A DNS component answered with an untrue IP address.

items.label: archive
items.desc: Data archived from the phishing server goes in ArchivedData.

items.label: ext-value
items.desc: An unidentified FraudType, captured in the ext-value attribute.

viz.caption: SENSOR TYPES THAT CAN DETECT A PHISH (RFC 5901, SECTION 5.10.1)

items.label: web
items.desc: A web server or service detected the event.

items.label: webgateway
items.desc: A proxy, firewall or other network gateway detected it.

items.label: mailgateway
items.desc: Detected via a mail gateway or filter.

items.label: browser
items.desc: Detected at the user web interface or browser.

items.label: ispsensor
items.desc: Detected by an automated network system such as an IDS or IPS.

items.label: human
items.desc: A person or manual analysis detected it.

items.label: honeypot
items.desc: Detected by receipt at a decoy device.
